set.approach: Start at the Horse Creek trailhead behind the Mono Village resort at Twin Lakes and follow the Horse Creek Trail up the drainage and through the meadows. Where the trail climbs to a shallow col, leave it for a use trail up the ridge east of the glacier drainage to a small lake just under 10,000 feet, which has several campsites. Continue up the moraine ridge to the toe of the Matterhorn Glacier, cross its short, nearly flat lower edge, and contour to the East Couloir, the higher of two ways onto the east ridge, in the gap on the left side of the peak.
set.descent_text: The normal way down is the approach route: reverse the couloir (snow in winter and spring, loose scree and a mixed scramble by late summer), cross the glacier edge and drop the moraine ridge to the lake and the Horse Creek Trail. From the top of the couloir the summit is reached by third-class ledges on the east ridge or by traversing round to the easier south side, so downclimb the same ground. A shortcut down the southeast slopes toward upper Horse Creek exists, but the trail there is faint and easily lost in talus, and it is usually slower than the standard line. Carry an axe and crampons while the couloir holds snow.

review.notes: MP: Horse Creek TH, couloir is the higher way to the east ridge, same approach as North Arete which is also the normal descent route; Outbound: lake, glacier, couloir gap left of peak, class 3 east ridge or south side; Mts Are Calling: trail, col, lake just over 9800, moraine, short glacier crossing, SE slopes shortcut poor trail, returned by standard route.

set.approach: Park at the gate on San Antonio Falls Road, off Mount Baldy Road (about 6,200 feet), and walk the road about half a mile to where a faint trail leaves the left bank. Follow it up the scree and onto the shoulder of the ridge to the Sierra Club Baldy Ski Hut at roughly 8,100 to 8,200 feet. From the hut a use trail or snow track crosses the bottom of the bowl west toward the low point on the ridge; the trail can be hard to follow in a big snow year. The Upper South Ridge begins from that col, as the left skyline seen from the hut.

review.notes: MP route page and HPS 16E Route 2 agree on gate, half mile of road, faint left-bank trail, Ski Hut at ~8100-8200, use trail west across bowl to south ridge. No descent written: neither source states one for this ridge.

set.approach: Park at the gate on San Antonio Falls Road off Mount Baldy Road and walk the road up to Baldy Notch, or ride the ski lift to the notch when it is running. Do not climb the slope under the lift, which is not permitted. From the notch follow the ridge road, then the trail, onto the Devil's Backbone, which runs east to west toward the summit.
set.descent_text: Return the way you came along the Devil's Backbone to Baldy Notch and the road or lift, as the ridge is the usual way down. When Harwood's snowfield blocks the ridge on the way up, the route skirts its lower southern edge to the saddle below Baldy's final slope. In winter the ridge carries ice, deep drifts and cornices above long slopes on both sides, and it has caused fatal falls, so an axe and crampons and sound judgment about conditions are needed.

review.notes: MP DB: road/lift to notch, ridge, skirt Harwood snowfield south edge, ice/cornices in winter, 'head back down'; MP NE Face: DB is the best way down to the car; HPS 16E/16J: gate, road to notch, no hiking under lift, winter danger and deaths.

set.approach: Start at Stockton Flat, where a gate crosses road 3N06 as it turns south toward Baldy Notch. Park near the gate and walk up the canyon to the west, taking the main fork that goes straight or right; the left fork leads to the northeast face of Harwood. Continue up the canyon until the broad gully and face come down directly above you, then climb it to the summit.
set.descent_text: The easiest way down is the Devil's Backbone, which returns to the gate at the start. From the summit follow the Backbone east, go down past the ski runs, and keep to the ridge that ends at the locked gate. Take care on that ridge: it splits several times, and wandering off either side runs into cliffs and loose rock. In winter the Backbone itself has ice and cornices above long slopes, so carry an axe and crampons.

review.notes: Approach and descent ridge detail rest on the MP NE Face page alone; the Devil's Backbone winter hazard is confirmed by MP DB and HPS 16E.

set.approach: Begin at Whitney Portal, at about 8,360 feet and 13 miles west of Lone Pine, and runs roughly 11 miles to the summit with more than 6,000 feet of gain. It climbs gentle switchbacks and stream crossings to Lone Pine Lake, where the Whitney Zone permit requirement applies, then passes Outpost Camp and Mirror Lake, climbs above treeline past Trailside Meadow, and reaches Trail Camp, the usual overnight camp and a water source. From there the switchbacks climb to Trail Crest on the Sierra crest, and the trail turns north along the ridge to the summit plateau. In spring and early summer an axe and crampons are needed on the upper trail.

review.notes: NPS: Whitney Portal start, 8,360 ft, Whitney Zone permits for all entering incl. day hikers, axe/crampons spring and early summer, ~10.7 mi; Wikipedia: 11 mi, over 6,100 ft gain, switchbacks to crest, traverses ridge to summit plateau; Peakseeker: Lone Pine Lake, Outpost Camp, Mirror Lake, Trail Camp water. Descent already present on the row; only approach written.

set.approach: The usual way in is from the Horseshoe Meadows trailhead, west on the Cottonwood Lakes trail past the lakes and up switchbacks to New Army Pass at about 12,300 feet. Long Lake is a common overnight camp. The trail beyond the pass heads on toward Rock Creek, so leave it there and turn right across the open, sandy ground to Langley's south slopes. About three miles of cross-country remain from the pass, ending on a long sandy slope below the summit block.
set.descent_text: Come down the way you went up. Drop the scree and sand of the south slopes to the pass and return to Horseshoe Meadows by New Army Pass, or by Old Army Pass, whose trail drops past Cottonwood Lake 4. The route is a walk-up with no rope work, but snow in spring can call for an axe.

review.notes: MP: standard walk-up, New Army Pass from Horseshoe Meadows (12,280), ~3 mi from pass, camp at Long Lake. 14ers report: Cottonwood Lakes, New Army Pass, pass trail continues toward Rock Creek, sandy slope to summit block, descended via Old Army Pass past Cottonwood Lake 4.

set.approach: Start at the South Fork trailhead on Jenks Lake West Road, off Highway 38 near Angelus Oaks, at about 6,850 feet. Follow the South Fork Trail (1E04) up past the Dry Lake fork at Slushy Meadows, then bear right at the fork to Dollar Lake at roughly 9,500 feet. The climbs on Charlton head up from Dollar Lake, and the couloir is on the north face above it. The trail beyond the lake continues to Dollar Lake Saddle, the usual way to the summit when the couloir is not in condition.

review.notes: HPS: South Fork TH 6850, trail 1E04, Dry Lake fork, Dollar Lake fork 9520, saddle; MP area: South Fork trail, Dollar Lake Saddle ~9500, climbs head up from Dollar Lake. Couloir location from MP/polyploid; no descent source read.

set.approach: Start from the Faye Luther trailhead off Fairview Lane (Route 206), south of Minden, Nevada. Take the trail to the first junction, then the fork signed for the Jobs Peak Ranch trail, and look for a faint path leaving on the left a short way past the second junction. A cairned use trail follows the right side of the gully for about half its height. The gully leads up to the east peak, a false summit northeast of the main summit, and the east ridge continues on to the top. Snow lingers in the gully through spring.

review.notes: MP area page: Faye Luther TH, junctions, faint path left, gully to east peak then east ridge; Climber.org: Faye Luther, Jobs Peak Ranch trail fork, cairned use trail on right side to half height, gully to false summit then ridge. No descent written.

set.approach: Start at the Brewer Creek trailhead (about 7,300 feet) on the quiet east side of the mountain. The trail is faint and disappears under snow, so head up toward the summit, which stays in view, along the open slopes south of the Brewer Creek drainage. The usual camp is a rocky bench at about 9,800 feet; Brewer Creek runs nearby and is typically open by mid-spring. The route climbs the broad snowfield above the camp between the Hotlum and Wintun glaciers, so recognise the start by the large snowfield rising straight above the bench.
set.descent_text: Descend the line you climbed. From the summit, angle down the steep upper chute and onto the Wintun side, where the slope is steepest and a fall can slide a long way, so keep the axe in hand and do not glissade carelessly. Cross back over the rib to the snowfield between the glaciers, below the high traverse, then run down the snowfield to the bench camp and the Brewer Creek drainage to the trailhead. The route has no major crevasses or fumaroles, but the snow can turn to heavy slush in the afternoon.

review.notes: Climber.org: Brewer Creek TH, no real trail, camps 9.6-10.4k, snowfield, descent via summit chute and Wintun glacier then crossing the ridge lower and down Brewer Creek; ASJ: TH 7,300, bench ~9,800, snowfield between glaciers, steepest near summit, slush; MP Hotlum Glacier: Brewer Creek TH, descend Wintun-Hotlum ridge. No permit or fee text.
